newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Europe looks to embrace east after sealing EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: Europe looks to embrace east after sealing EMU pact.

text.p: The European Union, fresh from sealing a landmark pact for its planned single currency, launched an attack on drugs and crime on Saturday and prepared to open the door to new members from the former communist east.
Meeting in a summit in Dublin, EU leaders also unveiled an urgent campaign to combat the menace of unemployment in the 15-country bloc.

The Irish hosts of the two-day meeting had set an ambitious target of mapping out the future shape of the European Union by securing the deal on the currency and taking forward negotiations on a new treaty preparing for the 21st century.
"It was a good summit...which pushed Europe forward," said Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene.

After winding up the summit's formal business, the EU leaders turned to the thorny issue of expansion as leaders of a host of new countries clamouring to join the Union gathered in Dublin for a foretaste of EU meetings of the future.
The EU leaders met government heads from Poland, Hungary, the Czech republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Romania and Cyprus.

All these nations have been offered the chance of joining the Union some time soon. Formal discussion on their membership are due to start in about one year's time, about six months after the new treaty is ready.

The new treaty is needed to cope with the flood of new members and one of its key aims will be to simplify decision-making, increasing the use of majority voting and stamping on vetoes by individual states.
The EU also wants to move forward on opening up the borders within Europe, while tightening up on security to make sure this new openness does not provide easy loopholes for criminals.

British Prime Minister John Major, possibly attending his last summit before an election, due by May, that he is expected to lose, has been adamant in his rejection of both giving up the veto and opening up Britain's borders.
"We are not prepared to surrender the veto," Major said on the last day of the summit.

Britain put its partners on notice that it would continue to oppose many proposals in the inter-governmental conference (IGC), the negotiations for the new treaty destined to be approved at a summit in Amsterdam next June.

Deeply worried about a European jobless rate of over 10 percent, twice as high as in the United States, the EU leaders used the Dublin summit to launch a declaration on employment, outlining the steps that were needed to create new jobs.

They called for enhanced labour market efficiency, more "employment friendly" taxation and social protection systems, efforts to modernise goods and services markets and steps to boost Europe's competitiveness.
The EU leaders also agreed a joint action plan to boost cooperation between police, customs and judicial authorities in fighting drug addiction and illegal drug trafficking.
Their joint declaration stressed the bloc's determination to fight organised crime and its "abhorrence" at the "odious" sexual exploitation of children and trafficking in humans.
The EU also issued a hard-hitting statement condemning Israeli settlements as a barrier to peace in the Middle East and calling on Israel to ease the block on Palestinian territories.
In a move likely to upset Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the EU instructed its special envoy to the region to promote these demands as immediate measures.

The EU also called on Yugoslavia to "demonstrate full respect for human and minority rights and the observance of democratic norms" and set conditions for sending international observers to check the regularity of the country's recent disputed local elections, including the right to re-run them.
The crowning achievement of the summit was the sealing of the pact to enforce fiscal rigour under the future single currency, aimed at ensuring the euro is as tough as the German mark.
Under the deal, countries would face penalties for running deficits of more than three per cent of gross domestic product unless they could prove their economies were suffering a severe recession.
